sections.content: You know *estar* for places and temporary states from A1 Unit 9, and the *ser* passive from B1 Unit 18. *Ser* + participle tells the action: someone closed the door. *Estar* + participle tells the result: the door is shut now. *La puerta fue cerrada a las ocho* (the action happened at eight) but *La puerta está cerrada* (you can see it shut). It works because a finished action leaves something behind, and *estar* describes what is there. The participle is still like an adjective and agrees with the subject: *las puertas están cerradas*.

sections.title: Action and result
rows: The road was closed yesterday. (the action)
The road is closed. (the result, now)
Cuando llegamos, la tienda ya estaba cerrada.
When we arrived, the shop was already closed. (the result, then)
The tickets are sold out. (the result)
Las calles están inundadas desde el lunes.
The streets have been flooded since Monday. (the result)

items.spanish: El museo fue clausurado en junio y sigue cerrado.
items.english: The museum was closed down in June and is still shut.

items.spanish: Los cuadros están dañados por el agua.
items.english: The paintings are damaged by the water.

sections.content: With *estar* you almost never add *por* and a doer, because you are looking at the result, not at who did it. To say who did it, go back to *ser*: *fue cerrada por la policía*. A time word like *ya*, *ahora* or *desde* points to a result: *ya está terminado*, *desde ayer está cerrado*.
